narrative: The model estimates a 67% chance that you will leave your job, which is why the promotion decision was negative: it treats your retention risk as too high to advance now. The strongest factor increasing that risk is your total work experience of 6–10 years; among employees predicted to stay, about 35% fall in this band, but for your profile it is the leading signal of departure. The next most influential factor works in your favor: you reported no other job opportunities, and this is common among employees predicted to stay (about 77%), so it lowers the leave risk. Your tenure with your current organization—1–5 years, as for about half of stayers—is the third most important factor, and it still pushes the prediction toward leaving. Other profile signals also matter: a low salary band, no bonus, low organizational support, no recognition, no deserved promotion, no job stability, and dissatisfaction with pay relative to effort all point toward disengagement and leaving. Because the model sees more evidence of flight risk than retention, promotion is denied. Next, you and your manager should discuss concrete retention levers: pay and bonus fairness, recognition, support, promotion pathways, and job stability. Because no outside opportunities were reported, there is a real chance to re-engage you before you begin looking elsewhere.
